transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yeah, thanks. So, honestly, my supervisor is the one who told me I needed to come see someone, because it's getting to be a huge issue at work. I work at a production plant, down on the line, and we have these specific stations we're assigned to, right? And you are absolutely supposed to stay put at your station because there's moving belts and forklifts and all this heavy machinery going around all the time. 

But I just... I keep leaving my station. Like, I'll just suddenly be up and walking away to check on something or look at a pallet before I even realize I've moved my feet. And it's not just out on the floor, it's in our morning meetings, too. We have these sit-down huddles in the breakroom at the start of every shift, and everyone is just sitting in these little metal folding chairs listening to the shift lead, and I just pop up. I'll just pop right up out of my seat to throw away a paper cup or pace around the back of the room, and I can't seem to just stay in the chair like everyone else. 

My supervisor pulled me aside yesterday and told me it's becoming a serious safety problem. He said I'm going to get myself hurt or get clipped by a machine because I just take off before I even think about it. Like, there's literally no thought process of "I should stand up now," I just do it. And I really need this job, you know? The pay is decent and I didn't finish high school, so I really can't afford to get fired just because I can't stay in one spot when I'm supposed to. So that's... yeah, that's why I'm here.
Do you feel restless when you're sitting or standing still at work?

Oh, god, yes. Constantly. It's... it's like this crazy intense feeling. Like, okay, if I'm trying to just stand there by my machine, right? Just standing perfectly still like I'm supposed to, waiting for the line to cycle... it literally feels like there is this actual, physical pressure just building and building up inside my body. Like a soda bottle that got shaken up and the cap is about to pop off. And it gets to the point where I absolutely *have* to move. Like, my brain is just screaming at me that I have to pace around my station, or stretch my legs out, or just go find something to do right that exact second. I can't ignore it. 

And it's exactly the same thing if they make us sit through those long training videos, like the quarterly safety stuff they make us do? I'll be sitting there trying to watch the screen, and my skin just starts crawling, and that pressure just ramps up in my chest and my arms, and I'm just thinking, "If I don't move right now, I'm going to crawl out of my own skin." So I have to move, or pace, or go do something right then. It's not like I'm just bored with the video or trying to be difficult, it's like an actual physical need to do something because that pressure gets so unbelievably bad and I just can't keep it pushed down.
Do you feel this restless and have the urge to move when you're not at work?

Honestly, I don't really know if I feel it when I'm not at work, because I don't really... stop? Like, I'm never just sitting around at home trying to be still, you know? When I'm off the clock, I'm always doing something. I'm cleaning the apartment, or I'm walking to the store, or I'm out doing something with my friends, or I'm fixing something. Like last weekend, I decided to completely reorganize my kitchen cabinets at two in the morning because I just couldn't sleep and I needed to be doing something with my hands. 

So I guess I don't really get that same exploding soda bottle feeling at home, but maybe that's just because nobody at home is telling me I have to stand in a three-by-three square for eight hours. If I want to get up and pace around my living room while I watch TV, I just do it. I don't even really think about it. I just... I'm always moving anyway. So I don't know if the urge is there, because I never really try to fight it when I'm on my own time. I just let myself go wherever my feet take me, I guess. So, yeah, I'm not really sure if it happens outside of work. I haven't really noticed it.
Did you feel restless or have trouble sitting still when you were a kid?

Oh, wow, yeah. Like, absolutely. It's funny you ask that, because honestly, looking back, it's always been this way. Even way back in elementary school, I was totally that kid. You know the one. Like, I remember being in Mrs. Gable's second-grade class, and she had this big, colorful rug where we were all supposed to sit criss-cross applesauce for reading time, right? And I just... I couldn't do it. I'd be up on my knees, or I'd suddenly be standing up and walking over to look at the class hamster, completely forgetting that we were right in the middle of a story. 

And it wasn't just getting out of my seat, either. I was constantly getting in trouble for talking. Like, the teacher would be explaining a math worksheet, and a thought would just pop into my head, and I would just blurt it out. I wouldn't even raise my hand, the words would just fall out of my mouth before my brain could stop them. I talked over the teachers all the time. My mom used to get so mad because I'd bring home these little behavior notes, like, constantly. They were always saying the same things: "She won't stay in her seat," "She blurts out answers," "She wanders around the room during quiet time." 

It was like my motor was just always running too fast, even back then. I remember one time in fourth grade, I got sent to the principal's office just because I couldn't stop tapping my pencils on the desk and then I got up to sharpen them like three times in ten minutes. I just... I couldn't sit there. So, yeah, it's definitely not a new thing, it's just that now it's happening at a job where there's forklifts instead of, you know, a hamster cage.
Do you often interrupt others when they're speaking?

Oh, man. Yeah. All the time. It's actually a huge problem for me at work, and it's so frustrating because I really don't mean to do it. It's like... okay, so if I'm on the floor, right? And I hear a couple of my coworkers talking over by the pallets, maybe they're trying to figure out how to stack a weird order or talking about something that happened on the previous shift. I'll just be walking by, and before I even realize what I'm doing, I'm just right in the middle of it. I'll just jump right into their conversation, completely uninvited, and start giving my opinion or telling them how I'd do it. And I can see the look on their faces, you know? That look that says, "Uh, who asked you?" But I just can't seem to stop myself. The thought is in my head, and it just has to come out right that exact second.

And it's even worse with the supervisors. Like, our line lead will be giving us instructions for the shift, or explaining a change in the process, and he'll be halfway through a sentence asking a question, and I'll just blurt out the answer before he's even finished talking. It's like my brain just jumps to the end of his sentence, and I feel this intense need to just say it. I don't even wait for a pause. I just cut right in. And then everybody gets so irritated with me. The lead will sigh and give me this look, and the other people on the line will roll their eyes, and I'm just standing there feeling like an idiot because I did it again. 

I try to tell myself, "Okay, just bite your tongue, let them finish, wait your turn," but it's like... it's like the words are burning a hole in my brain, and if I don't say them right then, I'm going to explode. It causes so much friction with the other workers. They think I'm being rude or a know-it-all, but I'm really not trying to be. It's just that impulse control thing, you know? It's just like when I was a kid blurting things out in class, only now it's grown adults getting mad at me instead of Mrs. Gable. It's just exhausting always feeling like I'm stepping on everyone's toes, but I honestly don't know how to stop it from happening.
Do you have trouble organizing your tasks or managing your time effectively?

I mean, I don't really think so? Like, at work, everything is already organized for me, you know? It's a production line. I just stand where they tell me to stand and do the thing they tell me to do until the buzzer goes off. There's not really any time to manage because the conveyor belt manages it for me. It's just... go, go, go. And at home, I just sort of do whatever I feel like doing whenever I feel like doing it. If I want to reorganize the kitchen at two in the morning, I just do it. I don't really have to plan it out or anything. 

I guess I'm not really the kind of person who uses planners or makes schedules or whatever. My mom always tried to get me to use those little agenda books in middle school, but I would just lose them or forget to write things down, so I gave up on that a long time ago. But I wouldn't say I have *trouble* with it now, because I just don't really have a lot of things that need organizing, if that makes sense? I just kind of live in the moment and deal with things as they come up. Like, if the rent is due, I pay it. If I need groceries, I go to the store. I don't really need a whole system for it. So, yeah, I wouldn't say that's a big issue for me. I just kind of roll with it.
Do you often find yourself easily distracted from the task at hand?

Oh, my gosh, yes. Distracted doesn't even begin to cover it. It's like my attention is just this bouncy ball that's constantly ricocheting off the walls. It's actually a huge issue on the production line, which is stressful because, like I said, it's just go, go, go, and you really have to pay attention to your own station. But I just... I can't filter anything out. 

Like, okay, picture this: I'm standing there, right? I'm supposed to be inspecting these parts as they come down the belt, and I'm trying to focus, I really am. But then, across the floor, maybe like fifty feet away, one of the other machines will make a noise. Just a beep, or a hiss, or whatever. And it's like my brain completely short-circuits. My eyes dart over there, my whole body wants to turn and see what's happening, and suddenly I'm not even looking at my own belt anymore. I'm just totally zeroed in on this random sound. 

Or, like, if somebody walks past with a pallet jack. It doesn't even have to be close to me! They could just be rolling by in the main aisle, and I'll just watch them. I'll watch the wheels, I'll look at what they're hauling, I'll wonder where they're taking it... and meanwhile, three or four parts have just sailed right past me on the belt without me even looking at them. It's so bad. And I know I'm supposed to stay on my own station, I know it's my job, but it's like every single little thing that happens in that warehouse is screaming for my attention all at once. 

It's not just big things, either. If a fly buzzes past my head, I'm watching the fly. If the person next to me shifts their weight or coughs, I'm looking at them. I just get pulled away so easily, and then it takes me a second to remember, "Oh, right, the belt, the parts, I'm supposed to be doing this." And by the time I snap back to it, I'm behind, and I have to rush to catch up, which just makes me more frantic. It's like I have no control over where my eyes go or what my brain decides to focus on. It just latches onto whatever the newest, shiniest, loudest thing is, no matter what I'm actually supposed to be doing.
Do you often interrupt others or blurt out answers when you're with friends or family, outside of work?

Oh, 100 percent. It's not just a work thing at all, it's literally my whole life. It’s exactly like what I was just saying, you know? How I cut in on people without meaning to, like jumping into my coworkers' conversations or answering a question before the lead is done talking, and then everybody gets irritated with me? It is the exact same story with my friends and my family. Honestly, they probably get even more annoyed because they've had to put up with it for so long. 

Like, just the other day, I was at my mom's house, and she was trying to tell me this whole long story about her neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, and some drama with the neighborhood watch or whatever. And my mom, she talks kind of slow, right? She really likes to build up the suspense and set the scene. So she’s pausing, and she’s like, "And then, you'll never guess who walked up to the driveway..." And I couldn't just wait the two seconds for her to say it! I just blurted out, "Was it the mailman? Was it Jerry?" And she just stopped dead, gave me this look, and sighed so loud. She was like, "No, if you would just let me finish a single sentence..." And I felt terrible! Because I actually did want to hear her story, but it's like I physically cannot handle the pause. 

And it happens with my friends all the time, too. We’ll be hanging out, maybe getting fast food or something, and my friend Jessica will be venting about her boyfriend. She'll be in the middle of pouring her heart out, and I'll just talk right over her to give her advice before she's even gotten to the actual point of why she's mad. Or I'll finish her sentence for her because she's taking too long to find the right word. And she gets so frustrated, she'll just throw her hands up and go, "Never mind, you're not even listening." 

But I am listening! I'm listening so hard that my brain is already ten steps ahead and I just have to get the words out. It sucks because I know it makes me look like a jerk who doesn't care about anyone else's feelings or what they have to say, but I really, really don't do it on purpose. It just slips out before I can bite my tongue, and then I'm just sitting there apologizing again.
Do you often act on impulse without thinking, like doing something reckless or spontaneous, when you're not talking to someone?

Um, reckless? Like, doing dangerous stuff? No, not really. I mean, I don't think I do. I'm actually pretty boring when I'm just by myself. Like, I definitely don't have the money to just go out and do crazy spontaneous things anyway. Working on the production line doesn't exactly pay for, like, random trips to Vegas or buying a car on a whim or whatever people do when they're being really reckless. 

The most spontaneous thing I do when I'm alone is maybe, I don't know, stopping at the gas station after my shift and deciding to buy a weird new flavor of energy drink instead of my usual one just to see what it tastes like. Or, like I was saying earlier, deciding to clean the kitchen or reorganize my closet at two in the morning. But that's not reckless, right? That's just kind of random. I'm not putting myself in dangerous situations or anything like that. 

Honestly, I'm kind of a homebody when I'm not at the warehouse. My feet hurt so bad after standing on that hard concrete floor for my whole shift that by the time I get home, I just want to crash. I'll just sit on the couch in my sweatpants and scroll on my phone for hours. There's not really any room to be reckless when you're just sitting there half-asleep, you know? I guess sometimes I'll get a sudden urge to, like, cut my own bangs in the bathroom mirror, and I've definitely done that a couple of times without really thinking it through. It always looks absolutely terrible, and I always regret it the next day when I have to bobby-pin it back for work, but it's just hair, it grows back. It's not like I'm out street racing or blowing my rent money on lottery tickets or something crazy. So, yeah, no, I wouldn't say I'm reckless at all. I just keep to myself mostly.
Do you have trouble waiting for your turn in lines or when doing group activities?

Um, waiting in lines? Not really, no. I mean, I don't think I do. I don't really mind it that much, to be honest. Like, nobody actually *likes* standing in line, obviously, but it's not like I'm losing my mind or getting super aggravated or anything. 

If I have to go to, like, Walmart or the grocery store after my shift, and it's super packed because everyone is getting off work at the exact same time, and they only have, like, two actual cashiers working because they want everyone to use self-checkout... I just get in line and pull out my phone. That's pretty much it. I'll just stand there with my basket and scroll through TikTok or Instagram for like fifteen, twenty minutes, just watching random videos of people doing makeup or whatever. I don't even really notice the time passing, honestly, because I'm just looking at my screen. Half the time, the line will move up and I won't even realize there's a huge gap in front of me until the person behind me clears their throat or nudges their cart forward, just because I'm so sucked into my phone. So, yeah, waiting isn't really a big deal for me as long as my phone is charged. 

And as for group activities... I don't really do anything like that. Like I was saying, my life is pretty much just the warehouse and my couch. On the production line, we aren't really taking turns, you know? We're all just doing our own thing at our own stations all at the exact same time. It's a continuous belt, so it's not like a "your turn, my turn" kind of setup, it's just a constant flow. And when I'm not at work, I'm just hanging out with my mom or maybe grabbing drive-thru with my friend Jessica. We aren't, like, playing board games or doing team sports or joining clubs or anything where I'd have to sit around and wait for somebody else to go. I just don't really put myself in situations where taking turns is even a thing in my day-to-day life. So, no, I haven't really noticed having any trouble with that at all.
Do you have trouble controlling your temper or getting into arguments with others?

Um, my temper? No, not really. I mean, I definitely wouldn't say I have a bad temper or anything like that. If anything, I'm kind of the opposite? Like, I avoid arguments like the plague. 

I know I was just saying how I interrupt people and annoy them, like with my mom or my friend Jessica, but when they get frustrated with me, I never, ever yell back or try to start a fight about it. I just immediately fold. I'll just be like, "Oh my gosh, I'm so sorry, I didn't mean to," and I'll just apologize a million times. Arguing literally makes my stomach tie up in knots, I hate it so much. I'm way more of a people-pleaser, I think. I just want everyone to be okay with me. 

Like, even at the warehouse, it can get really high-stress on the production line. Sometimes the belt gets jammed, or somebody further up the line messes up the count, and it throws everybody's numbers off for the whole shift. Some people get so mad. Like my supervisor, Gary, he will get bright red in the face and just start screaming at people over the noise of the machinery, and some of the guys will yell right back at him. But me? No way. I just keep my head down, keep my hands moving, and stay completely out of it. I don't want any drama. 

It was the same way back in high school, too, before I dropped out. You know how high school is, there was always some crazy drama going on, girls literally throwing hands in the cafeteria over a boy or a rumor or whatever. I never got involved in any of that. I was just trying to get through the day, honestly. I don't like confrontation at all. I feel like my brain is already going a million miles an hour just trying to keep up with normal life, so the idea of getting into a screaming match with someone just sounds completely exhausting. 

So, yeah, I definitely don't have a temper problem. I might be annoying because I talk over people or I get too excited and blurt things out, but I'm definitely not an angry person. I really can't even remember the last time I actually got into a real argument with somebody.
Do you find it hard to focus on one thing for a long time?

Oh, my gosh, yes. Like, it's actually a really big problem for me, especially at work right now. So, at the warehouse, sometimes they pull me off the main belt to do these inventory logs. And I know it's important to get the counts right, so I sit down with the clipboard and I tell myself, okay, just focus, get this done. And I start out really trying, I swear I do. I'll be checking the bins and writing things down, but after just a few minutes... I don't know, it's like my brain just hits a wall. I'll be staring right at the paper, and the numbers just start to blur together. 

And it's the exact same thing with this new training I'm trying to do. My supervisor Gary—the one I mentioned earlier who gets super red in the face and yells—he actually gave me this binder of CNC training pages because they're trying to cross-train some of us on the machines instead of just having us pack boxes. It would be a little bump in pay, which I really, really need, so I genuinely want to learn it. I'll sit in the breakroom on my lunch trying to read the manual, and I'll read the same exact paragraph like five or six times. The words just totally blur. I'll get all the way to the bottom of the page and suddenly realize I have absolutely no idea what I just looked at. I didn't take any of it in at all. 

So then I have to keep going back and starting over from the top, and I'll force myself to read it again, but by the time I finally get through one single section, my lunch break is already over. It's just so frustrating because I'm not stupid, you know? I mean, I know I dropped out of high school, but I know how to read perfectly fine. I just cannot keep my brain locked onto the page for more than a couple of minutes before it just slips away and I'm thinking about what I'm going to eat for dinner or some random video I saw online. It just takes me forever to get through anything like that. So, yeah, focusing on one thing for a long time is... it's really, really hard for me.
Do you find it hard to finish tasks because you lose interest or get distracted?

Um, finishing tasks? Honestly, no, I don't really think so. I mean, I know I literally just told you about how bad I am at reading that training manual for Gary, but that's kind of different, I think? Like, that's just me staring at paper and my brain checking out. But for actual tasks, like physically doing things? I pretty much always finish what I start. 

Like at work, on the line, you don't really have a choice. You can't just stop halfway through packing a box or sorting a bin because you got bored, you know? The belt is literally always moving, it never stops, so if you just decide you're over it and walk away or stop paying attention to your hands, the whole line gets backed up and boxes start piling up and falling off the end, and then everyone is screaming. So I definitely finish my tasks there. I just keep my hands moving and get it done until the buzzer goes off for break. 

And even at home, I don't really leave things half-done. Like, if I'm doing my laundry or something, I'll wash it, dry it, and throw it all on my bed. I might complain about it in my head, but I'll fold it all before I go to sleep because otherwise I wouldn't have anywhere to actually sleep! And my mom, oh my gosh, she would actually kill me if I started leaving half-finished projects all over our apartment. She is so strict about how the place looks. She has this whole specific way the kitchen has to be organized, for example. Like, if I decide to make a sandwich or something after my shift, I can't just leave the bread tie on the counter and the mayo sitting out because I got distracted or lost interest in cleaning up. I have to put the mayo back in the exact same little shelf on the fridge door, wipe the crumbs into the sink, rinse the knife... the whole routine. If I didn't finish doing all of that, she would lecture me for like an hour straight. So I just power through and get it done. I might be blasting music on my phone and, like, dancing around the kitchen while I do it to make it less boring, but I definitely finish it. 

So, yeah, I don't really have that problem where I just abandon things. I don't start a million different hobbies and drop them or leave half-painted canvases around or anything like that. My life is pretty basic anyway, just work and home, so there aren't really that many tasks for me to even lose interest in, to be honest. If I have to do something, I just do it until it's done.
Do you find it hard to focus or pay attention when you're doing things you enjoy, like hobbies or watching TV?

Um, no, actually. Not at all. If it's something I actually like doing, it's like the exact opposite of what happens with that training manual. I'm completely locked in. Like, I don't really have a lot of, you know, traditional hobbies, mostly because I'm always working at the warehouse or I'm just completely exhausted when I get home, but I really love watching TV. Especially reality TV or those crazy true crime documentaries? Oh my gosh, I can sit there for hours and not even realize how much time has passed. 

Like, just this past weekend, my mom went over to my aunt's place for the afternoon, so I had the apartment all to myself, which is super rare, right? So I figured I'd just chill on the couch and I put on this new docuseries on Netflix about this wild internet scam. And I swear to you, I started watching it at maybe one or two in the afternoon, and the next thing I know, I look at the window and it is pitch black outside. It was like eight o'clock at night. I hadn't even gotten up to get a glass of water or go to the bathroom or anything. I just watched all six episodes straight through, completely glued to the screen. I didn't even look at my phone once, which is saying something because Jessica is always texting me memes and stuff. 

So, yeah, if it's something I'm actually interested in, my brain has absolutely zero problem paying attention. It's only the boring stuff where my brain just hits that wall and shuts off. But if I'm scrolling on my phone watching videos or catching up on my shows, I'm totally, one hundred percent dialed in. Sometimes my mom actually has to physically wave her hand in front of my face to get my attention because I'm so focused on the TV and I literally don't hear her talking to me. So no, definitely no issue with that at all.
Have you ever been diagnosed with or suspected to have ADHD by a medical professional?

Um, no, actually. No doctor has ever said anything like that to me. I mean, to be totally honest with you, I haven't really been to a lot of doctors in my life anyway. Growing up, my mom was pretty much a single parent and she worked all the time, so we didn't exactly have the money or the insurance to just go to the doctor for every little thing. It was basically like, unless you were bleeding or had a fever of a hundred and four, you just toughed it out at home, you know? 

So, like, back when I was in school, before I ended up dropping out, I was always getting in trouble or falling behind, but none of the teachers or the school counselor ever suggested it might be a medical thing. They just acted like I was doing it on purpose, like I was just being a bad kid or I wasn't trying hard enough. It was always just, "She needs to apply herself," or I'd get sent to detention. Nobody ever stopped and said, "Hey, maybe we should have a doctor look at how her brain is working." My mom just thought I was being difficult and would ground me, and that was the end of it. 

And even now that I'm an adult, I don't really have a regular doctor that I go see for checkups or anything. If I get really sick, like if I get a bad sinus infection or something, I just go down to the urgent care clinic next to the strip mall by our apartment. And those doctors, they're always in such a huge rush. You wait in those uncomfortable plastic chairs for like two hours, and then they come in for five minutes, look in your throat, hand you a prescription for antibiotics, and rush you right back out the door. They definitely aren't sitting down and asking me deep questions about my life or how I'm doing at work or if I can pay attention to things. So there's never really been an opportunity for a professional to even notice anything, let alone diagnose me. 

Honestly, the only reason I'm even thinking about any of this now is just because I've been struggling so much at the warehouse, and my friend Jessica was actually the one who told me I should probably come talk to somebody. But yeah, as far as an actual medical professional diagnosing me or even suspecting anything? No, never. You're the first doctor I've ever really talked to about any of this stuff.
Did you experience these symptoms of restlessness, interrupting others, and difficulty staying focused when you were a teenager?

Um, a teenager? Yeah, definitely, but honestly, it started way before that. Like, way, way back. Even in elementary school, I was the kid who just... couldn't stay in my seat. Like, I was always *that* kid in the classroom. 

I remember, I think it was maybe second or third grade, my teacher actually put a square of masking tape on the floor around my desk to show me my "boundary" because I was constantly just getting up and wandering around the room. I didn't even realize I was doing it half the time! I'd just suddenly be over by the window looking outside, or I'd go sharpen my pencil for like the fifth time in an hour, or I'd just walk over to someone else's desk to see what they were doing because I was bored. Sitting still just felt physically impossible, like my legs had their own battery pack or something.

And the talking... oh my gosh, I was always in trouble for talking over the teacher. If they asked a question, I wouldn't even think to raise my hand, I would just blurt the answer out right in the middle of them still talking. Or if a random thought just popped into my head, I felt like I had to say it out loud right that exact second, even if it had absolutely nothing to do with whatever math or reading lesson we were supposed to be doing. I just couldn't hold it in. 

My mom was constantly getting notes sent home from my teachers about it, too. It felt like every single week I had some folded-up piece of paper shoved in my backpack that I was absolutely terrified to give her. They always said the same things—that I was being disruptive, blurting things out, wandering around, not focusing. And like I told you, my mom was a single parent working crazy hours, so she would get so, so mad when she had to deal with that stuff after a long shift. She'd yell at me, she'd ground me, take away the TV, everything. But no matter how much trouble I got into or how much I told myself I was going to be good and just sit quietly the next day, I literally couldn't stop doing it. 

So by the time I was a teenager in middle school and high school, it was just the exact same thing, just with harder classes and teachers who had way less patience for it. They didn't send notes home anymore, they just sent you straight to detention or the principal's office. Which is honestly a huge part of why I ended up dropping out. I just couldn't sit in those tiny desks all day listening to them drone on without feeling like I was going to literally jump out of my own skin, and I was always getting into arguments for interrupting them. So, yeah, it definitely wasn't just a teenager thing. It's pretty much been my whole life.
Have you ever lost a job, had relationship problems, or experienced other significant difficulties because of your restlessness, interrupting others, or difficulty staying focused?

Yeah. I mean, honestly, that's exactly what's happening right now and it's kind of the whole reason I'm even here freaking out about this. At work—at the warehouse, I mean—it's getting really, really bad. 

I was actually supposed to be on track to get my forklift certification soon. Which is a really big deal for me, because it comes with a pretty decent pay bump, and it means you don't have to just stand in one spot all day. My mom was so excited about it. But now, all of those certification plans are completely at risk, and honestly, my actual job is on the line, too. 

My supervisor, this guy Dave, he's already written me up a couple of times recently. He pulled me into his little glass office and gave me these official warnings for safety and production problems. Because I just... I can't stay at my packing station! I get so antsy standing in one spot for hours that my legs start aching, so I'll just wander off to see what Jessica is doing, or I'll completely zone out and mess up the shipping labels, which completely ruins our production numbers for the hour. And during the morning safety huddles, I'm always accidentally cutting Dave off when he's trying to explain the new protocols because I just blurt out whatever question pops into my head, and he gets *so* mad. He basically told me that if I don't get my act together and focus, I'm out the door. 

And it's not even just management that's mad at me, either. It's really affecting things with my coworkers, which sucks because I actually like them.
